sections.label: Overview
sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Haumiatiketike** ​(*haumiatiketike*) — ‌Wild Food, ‌Fernroot · ​Haumia ​tied to ​the earth ​— belongs ​to ‌the Polynesian ​tradition, where ​it ‌is catalogued ​under the ‌domain "Wild ​Food, ‌Fernroot". The ​name means ​"Haumia tied ​to ​the earth"[^1].

​**Haumia-tiketike** is ‌the Māori ​god ‌of uncultivated ​food — ‌the bracken ​fernroot ‌(aruhe) dug ​from the ‌wild with ​a ​digging stick, ‌the foil ‌to ‌his brother ​Rongo's planted ​kūmara. A ‌child ​of Rangi ​and Papa, ‌he hid ​within ​the earth-mother's ‌body when ​the world ‌was ​divided and ​never left ​it: wild ​food ‌belongs to ‌Papa herself, ​and cannot ‌be ​owned, only ​gathered.[^2]

PuniCodex ‌records ‌the canonical ‌scholarly spelling ‌**Haumiatiketike** and ​serves ‌its temple ​at [its ​temple](https://punicodex.com/haumiatiketike/). The ​displayed ‌form is ​ASCII-equivalent — ​a description ​computed ‌from the ​displayed form ​itself. The ​plain ‌ASCII form ​*haumiatiketike* contains ‌the same ​letters: ‌no recovered ​diacritics or ‌special ‌encoding is ​claimed. The ​work here ​is ​consistent citation, ‌capitalization, provenance, ‌and cultural ​context[^3].

sections.body:
The ​name is ‌attested in ‌modern Polynesian ​orthographies; macron ​usage ​follows each ​tradition’s reference ​dictionaries. Etymologically ‌the name ​means ​"Haumia tied ‌to the ​earth"[^1].

The ‌canonical spelling ​**Haumiatiketike** matches ‌the ​conventional scholarly ​romanization. The ​plain ASCII ​form *haumiatiketike* ​contains ‌the same ​letters, so ‌no lost ​diacritics or ‌encoding ​transition is ‌claimed. The ​editorial work ‌is to ​fix ​one reviewed ‌reference spelling, ‌preserve capitalization ‌and provenance, ​and ​keep the ‌original evidence ​visible. - ‌**haumiatiketike** — ​The ‌canonical ​restored ‌form Haumiatiketike.

​For ​the ​modern speaker, ​the ​closest ‌approximation ​is: Read ‌"Haumiatiketike" ​using ‌the reconstructed ​pronunciation ‌above; ​the ‌conventional Latin ​spelling ​adds ‌no diacritic ‌marks.

‌The ​conventional ​spelling "Haumiatiketike" ‌is ​already ​written in ‌Latin ​letters; ​the ‌lowercase form ​"haumiatiketike" ‌differs ​only ​in capitalization.

​The ​pronunciation ‌given above ‌reconstructs ​the ‌sound ​world in ​which ‌Haumiatiketike ‌was invoked. ‌Modern ‌speakers ​should ‌not expect ​exact ​identity ​with ancient ‌phonology; ​the ​reconstruction ​is a ‌scholarly ​compass, ​not a ​performance ‌prescription. ​The ‌reconstructed pronunciation ​of ‌Haumiatiketike ​is explained ‌separately ‌from ​its ​conventional Latin ​spelling, ​which ‌adds no ‌diacritic ​marks.

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
The ​stories of ‌Haumiatiketike ‌place ​wild food, ​fernroot ​at the ​center ​of ‌a living ​mythological ​world.

### Origins ‌(Myth)

​Haumiatiketike ‌appears in ​polynesian ‌tradition as ​wild ​food, ​fernroot. The ​name's ​meaning, "Haumia ‌tied ​to ‌the earth", ​shapes ‌the narratives ​told ‌about ​this figure.

### ‌Worship ​and Memory ​(Cult)

‌Devotees ‌and later ‌tradition-keepers ​preserved Haumiatiketike ​in ‌ritual, ​text, and ​iconography, ‌ensuring the ​name ​survived ‌into the ​modern ‌scholarly ​record.

The ​myths ​of Haumiatiketike ​survive ‌in ‌fragments, summaries, ​and ‌later retellings. ​Each ​version ‌reflects the ‌interests ‌of its ‌tellers ​— ‌poets, priests, ​philosophers, ​and scholars. ​The ‌PuniCodex ​entry does ​not ​privilege a ‌single ​version; ​it gathers ​the ‌attestations so ​that ‌readers ​can compare ‌them. ​The restoration ‌Haumiatiketike ‌gives ​the figure ​a ​stable name ​around ‌which ‌these variants ​orbit.

sections.body:
No ​monument, ‌inscription, ‌or artifact ​in ​the ​current ​PuniCodex ​corpus ‌is ​yet assigned ​to ‌Haumiatiketike ​with ‌certainty. ​That ‌absence ​should be ​read ​honestly: ​for ​a ‌Polynesian ​name ‌of this ​type ‌the ​material ‌record ​is ‌expected to ​be ​thin, ‌and ‌the ‌primary ​evidence ​remains the ‌textual ​testimony ​gathered ‌in ​the ​Scholarly ‌Sources section.

​Were ‌such ​evidence ​to ​surface, ​it ‌would take ‌recognizable ​forms: ‌votive ​or ​dedicatory ‌inscriptions ‌naming Haumiatiketike, ‌sanctuary ‌or ​cult ‌remains ​tied ​to wild ​food ‌and ​iconography ​matching ​its ‌traditional ​attributes (name ​and ​domain). ‌Each ​candidate ‌would ​be ‌weighed against ​the ‌reconstructed ‌form ​of ​the ​name ​before entering ‌the ‌scholarly ​record.

sections.label: Meditation & Reflection
sections.purpose: Contemplative or interpretive essay on the figure's enduring meaning.
sections.body:
Haumia-tiketike ​is the ‌god of ‌what the ​world gives ​freely ​and what ​we must ​still work ‌to ​receive. The ​fernroot was ‌never sown, ​never fenced, ‌never ​owned — ‌but it ​had to ​be found, ​dug, ​beaten, washed, ​and steamed ‌for hours ​before ‌it would ​feed anyone. ‌His is ​the theology ‌of ​uncultivated plenty: ‌generosity without ​cultivation, labor ​without ‌property. To ‌meditate on ‌Haumia is ​to ask ​where ‌your own ​food comes ​from — ‌not only ​the ​garden and ‌the market ​but the ‌ground ​itself, the ​wild margins, ​the places ​no deed ‌encloses.

‌He is ​also the ‌god who ​hid. While ​his ‌brothers warred ‌and were ‌eaten or ‌driven ​to sea, ‌Haumia chose ​the earth-mother's ​body and ​stayed ‌there, content ​to be ​the quiet ​portion ‌of the ​world's food. ​In a ​pantheon of ‌warriors ​and storm-gods, ‌the gentle ​one survived ‌by sheltering ​rather ‌than fighting ‌— and ​his reward ​was ​to become ​indispensable. The ‌wild root ‌outlasts the ​war.[^1]
